title: What expertise costs you
subtitle: The more fluent you become in design, the harder it gets to see what’s actually in front of you. That tension doesn’t resolve. It gets managed.

principles.headline: Expertise is a filter, not just a lens
body: The more you know about a domain, the more automatic your pattern recognition becomes. That’s efficiency — and it is also a kind of blindness. Senior designers have seen this problem before. They know what it looks like. They know what usually works. And that knowledge, if left unchecked, prevents them from seeing what’s unusual, unexpected, or genuinely new about the situation in front of them.

The curse of knowledge isn’t only about explaining things to non-experts. It’s about your own capacity to observe. When you’ve designed fifteen onboarding flows, the sixteenth begins to look like the others before you’ve read the brief. The pattern you recognize is the observation you didn’t make.
principles.callout: The pattern you recognize is the observation you didn’t make.

principles.headline: The beginner’s mind is a practiced skill
body: This is not about pretending you don’t know things. It is about maintaining the discipline of setting aside what you know long enough to see what is actually there. In Zen practice, this is called shoshin — the beginner’s mind. In research, it is called neutrality. In design, it is the difference between seeing an interface and seeing the person who uses it.

Cultivating this doesn’t require forgetting your expertise. It requires noticing when your expertise is doing the looking for you — and making a deliberate choice to slow down and let the problem speak. The most experienced designers aren’t the ones who have stopped asking obvious questions. They’re the ones who still do.
principles.callout: You can’t hear what the problem is saying if you already think you know.

actions.title: Name your assumptions before opening any tool
actions.desc: Before your first design session of the day, write down every assumption you’re bringing to the work. Not to challenge them — just to name them. Assumptions you can see are assumptions you can question.
actions.example: “I’m assuming users will read the confirmation screen. I’m assuming the biggest problem is discoverability. I haven’t confirmed either of these.”

actions.title: Explain the problem to someone who knows nothing about it
actions.desc: Find someone outside your project — a colleague from a different team, a friend, anyone without context. Explain the problem you’re solving. Notice where you stumble, where you use jargon, and where their questions reveal what you’ve stopped questioning.
actions.example: “They asked ‘but why would someone want to do that in the first place?’ — and I realized I’d never actually answered that question myself.”

actions.title: Look at something familiar for ten minutes without editing instinct
actions.desc: Pick a screen, a flow, or a product you have worked on or reviewed many times. Look at it for ten minutes with no intention to fix it. Just observe. Notice what you see when you’re not looking for problems to solve.
actions.example: “I watched the loading state for the first time in months. I’d always thought of it as neutral. I realized it’s actually the most anxious moment in the whole flow.”

actions.title: Ask one ‘obvious’ question today
actions.desc: In your next design review or team meeting, ask the question that feels too basic to say out loud. The one you’ve been assuming everyone already knows the answer to. Those questions are frequently the most clarifying ones in the room.
actions.example: “I know this might seem basic — but what does success actually look like for this feature? Not metrics. What does it look like for the person using it?”

actions.title: Name the pattern before you trust it
actions.desc: When you recognize a familiar pattern in a new problem, write it down explicitly: “This looks like a [navigation problem / trust problem / discoverability problem].” Then spend five minutes looking specifically for evidence that it isn’t. That friction is where the real insight often lives.
actions.example: “I immediately read this as a content hierarchy problem. When I forced myself to look for evidence it wasn’t, I found three users trying to do something the flow had never been designed for.”

coda.quote: Expertise earns authority. Beginner’s mind earns insight. You don’t get to choose one and skip the other — you need both, in tension, always.
coda.footer: The most useful thing your experience gives you is the ability to notice when it’s working against you.

closingQuote.text: In the beginner’s mind there are many possibilities, but in the expert’s mind there are few.
